name: Operating Systems viva bank
subject: Operating Systems
description: Processes and threads, CPU scheduling, synchronisation, deadlocks, memory management and virtual memory, file systems. Each question carries key points, follow-ups, a non-revealing hint and misconceptions.

questions.question: To start, tell me in about a minute about a project or program you have built, and one place where it had to deal with files, processes, threads or memory.
questions.rephrase: Describe any project you built and your role in it.

key_points.point: Says what the project does
Mentions an OS-level concern (threads, processes, files, memory)
Explains own contribution

follow_ups.text: Did anything in that project run concurrently? How did you make sure two parts didn't interfere?

key_points.point: Mentions locking/synchronisation or isolation

hints: Tell me a little more: what did it do, what data did it keep, and which part did you build yourself?

questions.question: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
questions.rephrase: How is a thread different from a process in terms of memory and resources?

key_points.point: A process is a program in execution with its own address space
Threads of a process share code, data, heap and open files
Each thread has its own stack, registers and program counter
Threads are lighter: cheaper to create and switch

follow_ups.text: If threads are cheaper, why would you ever use multiple processes instead?

key_points.point: Isolation: a crash or bug in one process doesn't corrupt others
Avoid shared-memory bugs / language locks (e.g. Python GIL)

hints: Think of a browser: each tab versus the different jobs inside one tab.

questions.question: What is a context switch, and why is it considered overhead?
questions.rephrase: What happens when the CPU switches from running one process to another?

key_points.point: Saving the state of the current process and loading the next one
State is stored in the process control block
No useful work is done during the switch (overhead); caches/TLB get cold

follow_ups.text: Why is switching between threads of the same process usually cheaper than switching between processes?

key_points.point: Same address space: no page-table/TLB switch

hints: Think of a teacher handling two classes at once: what must they note down before switching rooms?

questions.question: Explain round robin scheduling. How does the choice of time quantum affect it?
questions.rephrase: How does round robin decide which process runs next, and what changes if the time slice is very small or very large?

key_points.point: Each process gets a fixed time slice in cyclic order (preemptive)
Too small quantum: too many context switches / overhead
Too large quantum: behaves like FCFS, poor response time
Good for time-sharing / fair response time

follow_ups.text: With four processes and a quantum of 4 milliseconds, what is the maximum time a process waits before it gets the CPU again?

key_points.point: About 12 ms: (n minus 1) times the quantum, plus switch overhead

hints: Picture a whole class sharing a single lab computer, with a teacher keeping time.

questions.question: What is a race condition, and what is a critical section?
questions.rephrase: Why can two threads updating the same variable produce a wrong result, and how do we protect that code?

key_points.point: Result depends on the timing/interleaving of concurrent threads
Critical section: code accessing shared data
Only one thread at a time may execute it (mutual exclusion)
Protected with locks/mutex/semaphores

follow_ups.text: Why is count++ not safe across two threads even though it is a single line of code?

key_points.point: It is read, modify, write: three machine steps that can interleave

follow_ups.text: What are the three requirements a correct critical-section solution must satisfy?

key_points.point: Mutual exclusion
Progress
Bounded waiting

hints: Think of two people editing the same line of a shared document at the same moment.

questions.question: What is the difference between a mutex and a semaphore?
questions.rephrase: When would you use a counting semaphore instead of a mutex lock?

key_points.point: Mutex: one owner at a time, released by the thread that locked it
Semaphore: integer counter allowing up to N concurrent holders
wait/P decrements and signal/V increments (blocks at zero)
Semaphores also used for signalling/ordering between threads

follow_ups.text: How would you use semaphores to solve the producer-consumer problem with a bounded buffer?

key_points.point: empty semaphore initialised to buffer size, full to 0
Mutex protects the buffer itself

hints: Think of a parking lot with a fixed number of spaces versus a single-key washroom.

questions.question: What are the four necessary conditions for a deadlock?
questions.rephrase: Which four conditions must all hold at the same time for processes to deadlock?

key_points.point: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
No preemption
Circular wait

follow_ups.text: Which of these conditions is usually easiest to break in a real program, and how?

key_points.point: Circular wait: acquire locks in a fixed global order

hints: Picture four cars at a four-way junction, each waiting for the car to its right.

questions.question: What is paging, and what problem does it solve?
questions.rephrase: Why does the operating system divide memory into fixed-size pages and frames?

key_points.point: Logical memory split into fixed-size pages, physical memory into frames
Page table maps pages to frames
Removes external fragmentation; process memory need not be contiguous
Can cause internal fragmentation in the last page

follow_ups.text: Every memory access now needs a page-table lookup. How do systems keep this fast?

key_points.point: TLB caches recent translations
High hit ratio makes the average cost small

hints: Think of a hostel that gives rooms of exactly the same size, and a register that says which student is in which room.

questions.question: What is virtual memory, and what happens on a page fault?
questions.rephrase: How can a program use more memory than the RAM installed, and what happens when it touches a page that is not in RAM?

key_points.point: Gives each process a large address space backed partly by disk
Pages loaded on demand (demand paging)
Page fault: trap to OS, load page from disk into a frame, update page table, restart instruction
If no free frame, a page replacement algorithm picks a victim

follow_ups.text: What is thrashing and why does it happen?

key_points.point: System spends most time paging instead of executing
Too many processes / working sets don't fit in memory

hints: Think of how you work at a small study desk with a big bookshelf nearby.

questions.question: What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling? Give one algorithm of each kind.
questions.rephrase: Can the operating system take the CPU away from a running process? Explain both kinds of scheduling.

key_points.point: Preemptive: OS can interrupt a running process (timer, higher priority)
Non-preemptive: process runs until it blocks or finishes
Example preemptive: round robin, SRTF, preemptive priority
Example non-preemptive: FCFS, non-preemptive SJF

follow_ups.text: Why can shortest-job-first be unfair, and how is that usually fixed?

key_points.point: Long jobs can starve
Aging raises priority over time

hints: Think about whether a student can be stopped halfway through their presentation.

questions.question: What is an inode, and what information does it store?
questions.rephrase: In a Unix file system, where is a file's metadata kept, and what is in it?

key_points.point: Data structure holding a file's metadata
Stores size, owner, permissions, timestamps, link count
Stores pointers to the data blocks (direct and indirect)
Does not store the file name (names live in directories)

follow_ups.text: What is the difference between a hard link and a symbolic link in terms of inodes?

key_points.point: Hard link: another directory entry pointing to the same inode
Symbolic link: separate file containing a path; breaks if target deleted

hints: Think of the catalogue card for a library book: what is written on the card versus on the shelf label.

questions.question: What does the fork system call do? What are its return values?
questions.rephrase: How does a Unix process create a child process, and how do parent and child tell themselves apart?

key_points.point: Creates a child process that is a copy of the parent
Returns 0 in the child
Returns the child's PID in the parent, -1 on failure
Memory is copied lazily (copy-on-write)

follow_ups.text: Why is copy-on-write important for fork followed by exec?

key_points.point: exec replaces the memory immediately, so copying it would be wasted work

hints: After the call, two processes run the same next line. How does each one know which it is?

questions.question: Compare FIFO, LRU and optimal page replacement. Why is LRU used as a practical target, and how is it approximated?
questions.rephrase: Which page should the OS evict when memory is full, and why is true LRU expensive?

key_points.point: FIFO evicts the oldest page; can suffer Belady's anomaly
Optimal evicts the page used farthest in future: unrealisable, a benchmark
LRU evicts least recently used, exploiting temporal locality
Exact LRU too costly; approximated by reference bits / clock (second chance)

follow_ups.text: Why is exact LRU too expensive to implement in hardware for every memory access?

key_points.point: Would need to update a timestamp/stack order on every memory reference

follow_ups.text: What if a program scans a huge array once, larger than memory? How does LRU behave, and what could do better?

key_points.point: LRU evicts useful pages for pages never reused (scan pollution)
Scan-resistant policies: LRU-K, 2Q, ARC, MRU for scans

hints: Think about what information each algorithm would need to make its choice.

questions.question: Explain the Banker's algorithm. What does 'safe state' mean, and why isn't the algorithm used much in real operating systems?
questions.rephrase: How does the Banker's algorithm decide whether to grant a resource request?

key_points.point: Grants a request only if the resulting state is safe
Safe: some order exists in which every process can finish
Needs each process's maximum demand in advance
Impractical: max needs unknown, processes come and go, runtime cost

follow_ups.text: Is an unsafe state the same as a deadlock? Why or why not?

key_points.point: No: unsafe means deadlock is possible, not certain

follow_ups.text: What do real systems like Linux do about deadlocks instead?

key_points.point: Mostly ignore at OS level (ostrich); rely on lock ordering, timeouts, detection in DBs

hints: Think of a bank that lends money only when it is sure it can never get stuck.

questions.question: What is priority inversion? Describe how it happens and how it is solved.
questions.rephrase: How can a low-priority task end up blocking a high-priority task?

key_points.point: Low-priority task holds a lock the high-priority task needs
Medium-priority task preempts the low one, so high waits indefinitely
Solved by priority inheritance (or priority ceiling)

follow_ups.text: Can you name a real incident where priority inversion caused a failure?

key_points.point: Mars Pathfinder (1997) resets

follow_ups.text: Why does priority inheritance fix it?

key_points.point: The lock holder runs at the waiter's high priority, so medium tasks cannot preempt it until it releases

hints: You need three tasks of different priorities and one shared lock.

questions.question: How does a multilevel feedback queue scheduler work, and why is it a good fit for a general-purpose operating system?
questions.rephrase: How can a scheduler favour interactive programs without knowing in advance how long each job runs?

key_points.point: Several queues with different priorities and time quanta
Jobs that use their full quantum move down; jobs that block early stay high
Favours interactive/I/O-bound jobs without knowing burst lengths in advance
Periodic priority boost / aging prevents starvation

follow_ups.text: How could a clever program game a multilevel feedback queue, and how is that prevented?

key_points.point: Yield just before the quantum ends to stay at high priority
Account total CPU used at a level, not per burst

hints: Think about what the scheduler can observe about a job each time it gives up the CPU.

questions.question: What is journaling in a file system, and what problem does it solve after a crash?
questions.rephrase: Why do file systems like ext4 keep a journal?

key_points.point: Changes are first written to a journal/log before applying them
After a crash, replay or discard journal entries to restore consistency
Avoids long full-disk checks (fsck)
Metadata-only vs full data journaling trade-off

follow_ups.text: Why do many file systems journal only metadata by default, not file contents?

key_points.point: Journaling data writes everything twice: big performance cost
Metadata consistency is what keeps the structure usable

hints: Think about appending a block to a file: which on-disk structures change, and what if power fails between them?

questions.question: Two threads each run this function one million times on a shared counter. The expected final value is two million, but it often prints less. Reason aloud: why, and how would you fix it?
questions.rephrase: Why does this shared counter end up lower than two million, and how would you correct it?

key_points.point: counter++ is not atomic: read, increment, write can interleave
Updates are lost when both threads read the same old value
Fix with a mutex around the increment, or an atomic operation
Better: per-thread local counters combined at the end (less contention)

follow_ups.text: If you lock the mutex inside the loop, the program becomes much slower. Why, and what would you change?

key_points.point: Lock/unlock a million times plus contention/cache-line bouncing
Accumulate locally, lock once at the end

hints: Write out the machine-level steps of counter++ for each thread on paper, side by side.

questions.question: This bank-transfer code hangs forever under load. Explain what is happening and how you would fix it.
questions.rephrase: Two transfers between the same pair of accounts run at once and both freeze. Why?

key_points.point: Deadlock: thread 1 holds A waits for B, thread 2 holds B waits for A
Fix by acquiring locks in a global order (e.g. by account id)
Alternatives: trylock with backoff, or a single coarse lock

follow_ups.text: What happens with your ordering fix if someone calls transfer(A, A, 10)?

key_points.point: Locks the same mutex twice: self-deadlock unless handled

hints: Trace both threads step by step, assuming each gets exactly one lock before the other runs.

questions.question: A college server with 8 GB of RAM becomes extremely slow during exam results: the disk light stays on and CPU usage is low. Reason aloud about what is happening and what you would check and change.
questions.rephrase: The server is slow, the disk is constantly busy and the CPU is mostly idle. What is going on and how would you fix it?

key_points.point: Thrashing: constant paging/swapping because memory is overcommitted
Check memory and swap usage, page-fault rate (free, vmstat, top)
Reduce load: fewer worker processes, limit concurrency, kill memory hogs
Add RAM / cache results / fix leaks long-term

follow_ups.text: Why does the CPU look idle when the system is actually overloaded?

key_points.point: Processes are blocked waiting for disk I/O on page faults

follow_ups.text: What if you are not allowed to add RAM before results go live in one hour? What would you do?

key_points.point: Serve a precomputed/static results page; cap concurrent workers; queue requests

hints: Low CPU but a constantly busy disk: what is the CPU waiting for?
